beats.say: When a visible object moves across an image, its pattern often appears at different pixel coordinates. How could one tiny detector recognize the same edge in a different place? Start with this five-by-five image.

These three windows overlap. Two cross the brightness boundary; one sits entirely in the bright region. Predict which window should give our edge detector a zero response. We will build the rule and return to your prediction.
Each square stores a brightness value. Zero is dark; one is bright. The row and column tell us where that measurement belongs. A small window keeps neighboring pixels together.
Compare these two patches. Both contain the same total brightness. One is uniform, while the other has a boundary. Our detector needs a comparison across space to tell those arrangements apart.

A filter, or kernel, is a small table of weights. Subtract the left column. Ignore the center column. Add the right column. These hand-chosen weights, with zero bias, measure whether the patch becomes brighter toward the right.
Apply it to the uniform patch. The left side contributes minus two, and the right contributes plus two. Add them and the response is zero. Equal brightness on both sides cancels.

Now use the edge patch with the same total brightness. Its dark left side contributes zero. Its bright right side contributes three. The response is three. Backpropagation computes gradients for the filter weights, and an optimizer uses those gradients to update them. This signed rule makes our example inspectable.

Place the filter over the first window. Multiply each pixel by its matching weight, then add the products. Follow the highlighted pairs into the running sum. All nine terms belong to this one output position.
The total is three. Carry that result into the first cell of the feature map. Its position records which image window produced it. The kernel stays the same when we move to another window.
Look at the third window, filled entirely with bright pixels. Predict its response using the signed weights. Keep the value in mind while the next sweep fills the map.

The bright window gives zero: its two sides cancel. Now the window steps right, then down, and every response lands in the matching position. Watch the same nine weights remain beside the image throughout the sweep.

Moving one pixel at a time, with weights on adjacent pixels and no added border, only three starting rows and three starting columns fit. They produce a three-by-three feature map. Local connectivity limits each measurement to its patch; weight sharing lets one learned rule serve every valid location.

Keep the binary edge example intact. Now open the article’s separate four-by-four grayscale crop, with its bright central mark. Its horizontal ridge kernel has top and bottom rows minus zero point six, and a middle row one point one. These are supplied weights with zero bias, not a trained crack detector. Four minus three plus one gives two starting rows and two starting columns.

Build its upper-left response from the same nine aligned owners. The row contributions are minus zero point one one four, plus two point one one two, and minus one point one four six. Add them to obtain zero point eight five two. For any fixed placement, changing one weight changes the response by its aligned pixel multiplied by the weight change, with every other term held fixed.

Reuse that kernel over all four placements. The map is zero point eight five two, zero point seven eight nine, zero point eight one seven and zero point eight seven four. The bottom-right placement wins. PyTorch uses cross-correlation: stored weights are not flipped. Mathematical convolution flips both spatial axes. This symmetric ridge kernel happens to agree either way; an imported asymmetric kernel needs its intended orientation. Freely learned filters can absorb that flip into their coefficients, so the two conventions have the same representational capacity.

A two-hundred-twenty-four square RGB image has one hundred fifty thousand five hundred twenty-eight input values. A dense layer with two hundred fifty-six outputs needs thirty-eight million five hundred thirty-five thousand four hundred twenty-four parameters, including biases. Our sixteen three-by-three RGB filters need four hundred thirty-two weights and sixteen biases: four hundred forty-eight parameters.

Those two layers have different outputs: two hundred fifty-six global dense values versus sixteen two-hundred-twenty-two square maps. To isolate sharing, keep the convolution’s local output geometry fixed and give every position a private filter bank. Forty-nine thousand two hundred eighty-four banks times four hundred forty-eight parameters gives twenty-two million seventy-nine thousand two hundred thirty-two. Tie all those banks back to one shared owner, and the count returns to four hundred forty-eight.

Local connectivity chooses which neighboring inputs each output reads. Sharing chooses whether different output positions own separate parameters. Flattening itself can preserve all pixels and their recoverable order; the dense wiring does not enforce a reusable local detector. These parameter counts do not compare equal outputs or establish a speed ratio.

Move the boundary one pixel right. The same local comparisons now respond one column farther right. The old map stays faintly visible so you can follow the displacement. This corresponding movement is translation equivariance.

A global maximum keeps the largest response. Scan the actual cells into this accumulator. Both versions produce three here, even though their response locations differ. On a finite image, the border and sampling pattern still affect which comparisons exist.
Stride sets the distance between starts. Move two cells at a time. This image now permits four windows, giving a two-by-two output. We still use the same kernel at each selected position.

Return to stride one. Add one row and column of zeros around each side. At this upper boundary, the new zeros enter the patch. Two bright pixels contribute plus two on the positive side, and the negative side contributes zero, so this response becomes two. The border has changed the calculation.

Follow the selected window around several more boundary positions, then fill the remaining map. The output-size rule counts these complete placements. With unit dilation, insert the image size, padding, kernel size and stride into the displayed formula.

Stride changes the gap between starts. Dilation changes the gap between weights inside one placement. A three-by-three kernel at dilation two still has nine weights, but spans five-by-five positions. Its effective span is dilation multiplied by the quantity kernel size minus one, then plus one.

For each spatial axis, add padding on both sides, subtract that effective span, divide by stride, round down, then add one. For equal padding on both sides, the numerator is input size plus twice the per-side padding minus dilation multiplied by the quantity kernel size minus one, minus one. For unequal sides, replace twice padding with the sum of the two padding amounts. Divide the whole numerator by stride before taking the floor. Incomplete windows do not create outputs. At stride one, same-size padding adds a total of dilation multiplied by the quantity kernel size minus one extra positions, split across the two sides. An odd total requires unequal sides. Shape checks require positive kernel, stride and dilation, nonnegative padding, and a footprint that fits the padded input.

A color image has several input channels. Our small example uses two. One output filter has a kernel for each channel. Compute each patch sum, then add the contributions. Here, three plus three gives one output value of six. We use zero bias.

A second output filter gets its own weights. Negate the first channel kernel and retain the second. The channel contributions become minus three and plus three, so this filter gives zero at the same position. Multiple filters create multiple output maps.

With groups one, each output filter sees all input channels. Its stored shape is output channels by input channels by kernel height by kernel width. Add one bias per output filter. A batch keeps its own axis: batch, input channels, height, width becomes batch, output channels, output height, output width. This describes axis order, not a required physical memory layout.

Groups divides the input and output channels into separate connected sets. Each filter sees input channels divided by groups, and both channel counts must divide evenly by the group count. With four inputs, six outputs, two groups and three-by-three weights, each output reads two channels. Six times two times nine, plus six biases, gives one hundred fourteen parameters. Disconnecting the other group is a real change in the function.

In general the parameter count is output channels multiplied by input channels divided by groups, multiplied by kernel height and width, then plus output biases when enabled. Spatial size, stride and dilation change placements, not the number of stored coefficients in this layer. Multiple outputs mean separate filter stacks; summing their channels does not replace the output-channel axis.

A later activation reads earlier activations, so track their original pixel owners. Start with field one and jump one. Field is the side length of the theoretical input footprint. Jump is the spacing between neighboring activation centers in input pixels. Add dilation times the quantity kernel size minus one, multiplied by the old jump, to the field.
